Rhombic sulfur \((\alpha)\) and monoclinic sulfur \((\beta)\) are the two important allotropes of sulfur. Both are non-metallic and both are built from the same \(\mathrm{S_8}\) puckered-ring molecule; they differ in the way those rings pack, and hence in every bulk property:

| Property | Rhombic sulfur (\(\alpha\)-sulfur) | Monoclinic sulfur (\(\beta\)-sulfur) |
|---|---|---|
| Colour | Pale yellow | Bright yellow solid |
| Shape | Orthorhombic crystals | Needle-shaped monoclinic crystals |
| Melting point | 385.8 K | 393 K |
| Density | \(2.069\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\) | \(1.989\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\) |
| Solubility | Insoluble in water, soluble in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) | Soluble in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) |
| Stability | Stable **below** 369 K; above it changes into \(\beta\)-sulfur | Stable **above** 369 K; below it changes into \(\alpha\)-sulfur |
| Structure | \(\mathrm{S_8}\) molecules with a puckered ring | \(\mathrm{S_8}\) molecules with a puckered ring |
| Preparation | By evaporating a solution of roll sulfur in \(\mathrm{CS_2}\) | Rhombic sulfur is melted in a dish and cooled until a crust forms; two holes are made in the crust and the remaining liquid poured out, leaving needle-shaped crystals |

369 K is the transition temperature: it is the one temperature at which the two forms are in equilibrium.

(Table 7.7 prints the two densities as "2.069/ cm\(^3\)" and "1.989 / cm\(^3\)", omitting the mass unit; the unit is \(\mathrm{g/cm^3}\), as the corresponding column of Table 7.2 is headed.)

Sulfur in \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) is in its highest oxidation state, \(+6\), so the acid can only be reduced. Hot concentrated sulfuric acid oxidises both metals and non-metals and is itself reduced to \(\mathrm{SO_2}\), in which sulfur is \(+4\). Two reactions from the chapter:

**1. With copper (a metal):**

\(\mathrm{Cu} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\ (\text{conc.}) \longrightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_4} + \mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Copper is oxidised from 0 to \(+2\); sulfur is reduced from \(+6\) to \(+4\).

**2. With sulfur (a non-metal):**

\(\mathrm{S} + 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\ (\text{conc.}) \longrightarrow 3\mathrm{SO_2} + 2\mathrm{H_2O}\)

Here the free sulfur is oxidised from 0 to \(+4\) while the sulfur of the acid is reduced from \(+6\) to \(+4\) — both end up as \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).

**Preparation.** In the laboratory sulfur dioxide is prepared by treating an aqueous solution of sodium sulfite with dilute sulfuric acid:

\(\mathrm{Na_2SO_3} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Na_2SO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)} + \mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

The stronger, less volatile sulfuric acid displaces the weaker, volatile sulfurous acid from its salt, and the sulfurous acid at once breaks down to water and \(\mathrm{SO_2}\) gas.

**Two physical properties of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\)** (any two of the chapter's four):

1. It is a **colourless gas with a pungent smell**, and is poisonous.

2. It is **highly soluble in water**, and its solution in water is called sulfurous acid.

(Also: it liquefies at room temperature under a pressure of 2 atm, and boils at 263 K.)

Sulfuric acid is manufactured by the **Contact process**, in three steps.

**Step 1 — production of \(\mathrm{SO_2}\).** Sulfur, or a sulfide ore such as iron pyrites, is burnt or roasted in air:

\(\mathrm{S(s)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

\(4\mathrm{FeS_2(s)} + 11\mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} 2\mathrm{Fe_2O_3(s)} + 8\mathrm{SO_2(g)}\)

**Step 2 — catalytic oxidation to \(\mathrm{SO_3}\).** The sulfur dioxide is oxidised by oxygen over a vanadium pentoxide catalyst:

\(2\mathrm{SO_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{V_2O_5}} 2\mathrm{SO_3(g)}\)

This reaction is **exothermic and reversible**, and the forward reaction decreases the number of gas molecules, hence the volume. By Le Chatelier's principle a **low temperature (720 K)** and a **high pressure (2 bar)** therefore give the maximum yield of \(\mathrm{SO_3}\).

**Step 3 — absorption and dilution.** The \(\mathrm{SO_3}\) leaving the catalytic converter is absorbed not in water (which would give an unmanageable acid mist) but in concentrated sulfuric acid, giving oleum:

\(\mathrm{SO_3(g)} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{H_2S_2O_7}\ \ (\text{oleum})\)

The oleum is then diluted with water to give sulfuric acid of the required concentration:

\(\mathrm{H_2S_2O_7} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow 2\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\)

The sulfuric acid obtained by the contact process is 96–98 % pure.
